claim: The HIV-1 protease (HIV-1PR) cleaves human CARD8 between phenylalanine (F) 59 (P1) and F60 (P1').
source: The HIV-1 protease (HIV-1PR) cleaves human CARD8 between phenylalanine (F) 59 (P1) and F60 (P1') (Figure 1A; Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2021 and reference to Figure 1A showing the cleavage site.

claim: The amino acid P1 site, F59, is invariant among hominoids, gibbons, and Old World monkeys.
source: While the amino acid P1 site, F59, is invariant among hominoids, gibbons, and Old World monkeys, only human CARD8 has a phenylalanine at the P1' site, F60 (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic alignment data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Only human CARD8 has a phenylalanine at the P1' site, F60.
source: While the amino acid P1 site, F59, is invariant among hominoids, gibbons, and Old World monkeys, only human CARD8 has a phenylalanine at the P1' site, F60 (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic alignment data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The F59-F60 motif arose in the human lineage after the divergence of chimpanzees and humans.
source: The F59-F60 motif therefore must have arisen in the human lineage after the most recent common ancestor with chimpanzees and bonobos.
evidence: Inferred from phylogenetic analysis showing the motif is present in humans but not in chimpanzees or bonobos.

claim: The F59-F60 motif is present in Homo neanderthalensis (Neanderthal) CARD8.
source: The F59-F60 motif is also present in Homo neanderthalensis (i.e. Neanderthal) CARD8 (Figure 1A), conservatively dating its emergence within the last million years (Green et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic data in Figure 1A and citation to Green et al., 2010.

claim: The F59-F60 motif emerged within the last million years.
source: The F59-F60 motif is also present in Homo neanderthalensis (i.e. Neanderthal) CARD8 (Figure 1A), conservatively dating its emergence within the last million years (Green et al., 2010).
evidence: Based on citation to Green et al., 2010 regarding Neanderthal divergence timing.

claim: Wildtype human CARD8 with an N-terminal mCherry fusion is cleaved upon transfection of HIV-1 and HIV-2 proviruses, resulting in an ~33 kDa product.
source: Indeed, we found that wildtype (WT) human CARD8 with an N-terminal mCherry fusion is cleaved upon transfection of HIV-1 and HIV-2 proviruses, resulting in an ~33 kDa product (Figure 1B and C, top blot).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: The band at ~45 kDa is the result of cleavage by the 20S proteasome and results in a non-functional product.
source: The band at ~45 kDa is the result of cleavage by the 20S proteasome and results in a non-functional product (Hsiao et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hsiao et al., 2022.

claim: Cleavage of CARD8 by HIV proviruses is dependent on the protease encoded by the Gag-Pol gene.
source: Cleavage of CARD8 in these experiments was dependent on the protease encoded by the Gag-Pol gene of these proviruses as the HIVPR inhibitor lopinavir (LPV) blocked both Gag processing of p55gag to p41gag and p24gag and CARD8 cleavage (Figure 1C, top and middle blot).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing lopinavir blocks CARD8 cleavage, shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The HIVPR inhibitor lopinavir (LPV) blocks both Gag processing and CARD8 cleavage.
source: Cleavage of CARD8 in these experiments was dependent on the protease encoded by the Gag-Pol gene of these proviruses as the HIVPR inhibitor lopinavir (LPV) blocked both Gag processing of p55gag to p41gag and p24gag and CARD8 cleavage (Figure 1C, top and middle blot).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: HIVPR cleavage of WT human CARD8 (F60) is much more efficient than cleavage of human CARD8 F60L or F60S.
source: HIVPR cleavage of WT human CARD8 (F60) was much more efficient than cleavage of human CARD8 F60L or F60S (Figure 1D), consistent with prior findings that an alanine at position 60 also blocks HIVPR (Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 1D and citation to Wang et al., 2021.

claim: An alanine at position 60 blocks HIVPR cleavage of CARD8.
source: HIVPR cleavage of WT human CARD8 (F60) was much more efficient than cleavage of human CARD8 F60L or F60S (Figure 1D), consistent with prior findings that an alanine at position 60 also blocks HIVPR (Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2021.

claim: Species-specific variation at position 60 impacts CARD8 recognition of HIVPR activity.
source: These results indicate that species-specific variation at position 60 impacts CARD8 recognition of HIVPR activity.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing differential cleavage efficiency with different amino acids at position 60.

claim: SIVcpzEK505 and SIVcpzLB7 represent lineages that gave rise to HIV-1 group N and M viruses, respectively.
source: SIVcpzEK505 and SIVcpzLB7 represent lineages that gave rise to HIV-1 group N and M viruses, respectively (Barbian et al., 2015; Keele et al., 2006; Sharp and Hahn, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Barbian et al., 2015; Keele et al., 2006; Sharp and Hahn, 2011.

claim: Both SIVcpz proteases (SIVcpzPR) cleave human CARD8.
source: Like HIV-1 and HIV-2 proteases, we found that both SIVcpz proteases (SIVcpzPR) cleaved human CARD8 (Figure 2A), suggesting that SIVcpzPR had a pre-existing ability to cleave human CARD8 prior to spillover.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: SIVcpzPR had a pre-existing ability to cleave human CARD8 prior to spillover.
source: Like HIV-1 and HIV-2 proteases, we found that both SIVcpz proteases (SIVcpzPR) cleaved human CARD8 (Figure 2A), suggesting that SIVcpzPR had a pre-existing ability to cleave human CARD8 prior to spillover.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing SIVcpzPR cleaves human CARD8.

claim: SIVcpzPR does not cleave chimpanzee CARD8.
source: To deduce whether or not this cleavage is unique to humans, we also tested SIVcpzPR ability to cleave chimpanzee CARD8 (Figure 2A) and F60L and F60S human CARD8 variants (Figure 2B) and found that none of the other CARD8 variants could be cleaved by SIVcpzPR.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: SIVcpzPR does not cleave F60L and F60S human CARD8 variants.
source: To deduce whether or not this cleavage is unique to humans, we also tested SIVcpzPR ability to cleave chimpanzee CARD8 (Figure 2A) and F60L and F60S human CARD8 variants (Figure 2B) and found that none of the other CARD8 variants could be cleaved by SIVcpzPR.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: SIVmac239PR cleaves WT human CARD8.
source: Moreover, SIVmac239PR also cleaved WT human CARD8, an event that was greatly reduced when tested against the human CARD8 cleavage mutant F60A (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: SIVmac239PR cleavage of human CARD8 is greatly reduced when tested against the human CARD8 cleavage mutant F60A.
source: Moreover, SIVmac239PR also cleaved WT human CARD8, an event that was greatly reduced when tested against the human CARD8 cleavage mutant F60A (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The F59-F60 motif that arose in the human lineage renders human CARD8 uniquely susceptible to cleavage at that position by a broad range of primate lentiviral proteases.
source: Moreover, the F59-F60 motif that arose in the human lineage renders human CARD8 uniquely susceptible to cleavage at that position by a broad range of primate lentiviral proteases.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing multiple primate lentiviral proteases cleave human CARD8 but not other primate CARD8 variants.

claim: Some HIV-1PR is active in the cytoplasm.
source: However, we observed Gag processing of p55gag to p41gag and p24gag in cytoplasmic lysates of THP-1 cells infected with either WT HIV-1LAI or HIV-1LAI that was pseudotyped with the vesicular stomatitis virus glycoprotein (VSV-g) instead of its own envelope (HIV-1LAI-VSVG), consistent with prior studies demonstrating that some HIV-1PR is active in the cytoplasm (Figure 3A; Alvarez et al., 2006; Tabler et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 3A and citations to Alvarez et al., 2006; Tabler et al., 2022.

claim: HIV-1 infection and VbP treatment induce cell death in THP-1 cells compared to mock-infected controls.
source: For both HIV-1-infected and VbP-treated THP-1 cells, we observed an increase in cell death compared to mock-infected controls as measured by uptake of the membrane-impermeable dye propidium iodide (PI) (Figure 3B, left).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Neither HIV-1 infection nor VbP alone led to an increase in IL-1β levels in unprimed THP-1 cells.
source: However, neither HIV-1 infection nor VbP alone led to an increase in IL-1β levels (Figure 3B, right, no prime condition), consistent with prior reports (Ball et al., 2020; Linder et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 3B and citations to Ball et al., 2020; Linder et al., 2020.

claim: VbP specifically activates the CARD8 inflammasome in THP-1 cells.
source: As a positive control for inflammasome activity, uninfected cells were also treated with VbP, which specifically activates the CARD8 inflammasome in THP-1 cells (Johnson et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Johnson et al., 2020.

claim: VbP treatment and HIV-1LAI-VSVG infection induce cell death independent of priming.
source: We found that VbP treatment and HIV-1LAI-VSVG infection induce cell death independent of priming, although TLR agonists did elevate cell death responses in some instances (Figure 3B left).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The release of IL-1β after HIV-1 infection or VbP treatment is entirely dependent on TLR priming.
source: In contrast, the release of IL-1β after HIV-1 infection or VbP treatment was entirely dependent on TLR priming (Figure 3B, right).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: HIV-1 infection alone is sufficient to induce cell death in THP-1 cells.
source: Thus, HIV-1 infection alone (i.e. in the absence of molecules causing premature dimerization of Gag-Pol) is sufficient to induce cell death in THP-1 cells, and priming (e.g. via TLR stimulation) is required for HIV-1 infection-induced IL-1β secretion and elevated levels of cell death.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing cell death occurs without priming.

claim: Priming via TLR stimulation is required for HIV-1 infection-induced IL-1β secretion.
source: Thus, HIV-1 infection alone (i.e. in the absence of molecules causing premature dimerization of Gag-Pol) is sufficient to induce cell death in THP-1 cells, and priming (e.g. via TLR stimulation) is required for HIV-1 infection-induced IL-1β secretion and elevated levels of cell death.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing IL-1β secretion only occurs with TLR priming.

claim: IL-1β secretion, cell death, and CASP1 activation are significantly reduced in CARD8 KO versus WT THP-1 cells following HIV-1 infection.
source: Similar to our observations with VbP, we found that IL-1β secretion, cell death, and CASP1 activation (as measured by FLICA assay) were significantly reduced in CARD8 KO versus WT THP-1 cells following HIV-1 infection (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B (likely meant to be Figure 3C based on context).

claim: The inflammasome response to HIV-1 infection in THP-1 cells is primarily dependent on CARD8, but independent of HIV-1 envelope.
source: Because responses to HIV-1 infection were reduced to a similar level in both CARD8 KO cells and CASP1 KO cells, our findings suggest that the inflammasome response to HIV-1 infection in THP-1 cells is primarily dependent on CARD8, but independent of HIV-1 envelope.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data comparing responses in CARD8 KO and CASP1 KO cells.

claim: HIV-1Q23-BG505 infection results in IL-1β secretion in a CARD8-dependent manner.
source: HIV-1Q23-BG505 infection also resulted in IL-1β secretion in a CARD8-dependent manner, suggesting that CARD8-dependent inflammasome activation is conserved across HIV-1 strains.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: CARD8-dependent inflammasome activation is conserved across HIV-1 strains.
source: HIV-1Q23-BG505 infection also resulted in IL-1β secretion in a CARD8-dependent manner, suggesting that CARD8-dependent inflammasome activation is conserved across HIV-1 strains.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing multiple HIV-1 strains activate CARD8.

claim: There is a statistically significant, CARD8-dependent increase in IL-1β as early as 2 hr after HIV-1 infection.
source: Unexpectedly, we revealed a statistically significant, CARD8-dependent increase in IL-1β as early as 2 hr after infection (the first timepoint assayed after the initial infection), which plateaued for the next 6 hr and then further increased by 24 hr post-infection (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The early timepoints of IL-1β increase were sampled prior to reverse-transcription and the genesis of de novo synthesized HIV-1 transcripts.
source: As the early timepoints were sampled prior to reverse-transcription and the genesis of de novo synthesized HIV-1 transcripts (Mohammadi et al., 2013), these findings raised the possibility that CARD8 detects the activity of packaged HIV-1PR released into the target cell upon viral entry as well as de novo synthesized Gag-Pol.
evidence: Based on citation to Mohammadi et al., 2013 regarding timing of reverse transcription.

claim: CARD8 detects the activity of packaged HIV-1PR released into the target cell upon viral entry as well as de novo synthesized Gag-Pol.
source: As the early timepoints were sampled prior to reverse-transcription and the genesis of de novo synthesized HIV-1 transcripts (Mohammadi et al., 2013), these findings raised the possibility that CARD8 detects the activity of packaged HIV-1PR released into the target cell upon viral entry as well as de novo synthesized Gag-Pol.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing early IL-1β response before de novo viral protein synthesis.

claim: The HIVPR inhibitor LPV blocks CARD8 inflammasome activation by HIV-1 infection.
source: To test this hypothesis, we treated target cells with the HIVPR inhibitor LPV, which blocked CARD8 inflammasome activation by HIV-1 infection, reinforcing that CARD8 senses HIV-1PR activity.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: An HIV-1 virus lacking Vpr (ΔVpr) induces CARD8-dependent inflammasome activation.
source: However, we found that an HIV-1 virus lacking Vpr (ΔVpr) also induces CARD8-dependent inflammasome activation (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: HIV-1 infection induces inflammasome activation upon CARD8 detection of HIV-1PR released from the incoming virion as well as newly translated HIV-1PR.
source: Thus, our findings suggest that HIV-1 infection induces inflammasome activation upon CARD8 detection of HIV-1PR released from the incoming virion as well as newly translated HIV-1PR.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing early and late IL-1β responses and LPV inhibition.

claim: CARD8 KO THP-1 cells complemented with WT CARD8 undergo IL-1β secretion and cell death in response to both VbP and HIV-1 infection in a dox-dependent manner.
source: We found that CARD8 KO THP-1 cells complemented with WT CARD8 underwent IL-1β secretion and cell death in response to both VbP and HIV-1 infection in a dox-dependent manner (Figure 5B and C), confirming that HIV inflammasome activation is CARD8-dependent.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: All complemented CARD8 KO THP-1 cells undergo IL-1β secretion and cell death in response to VbP in dox-treated cells.
source: In parallel, we complemented CARD8 KO THP-1 cells with the CARD8 cleavage mutants F60L, F60S, F60A. All complemented CARD8 KO THP-1 cells underwent IL-1β secretion and cell death in response to VbP in dox-treated cells, demonstrating functional CARD8 expression (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: HIV-1LAI infection induces IL-1β secretion and cell death only in CARD8 KO THP-1 cells that were complemented with WT human CARD8, but not CARD8 mutants that are resistant to HIV-1PR cleavage.
source: In contrast, infection with both VSV-g pseudotyped (Figure 5B and C) and replication competent (Figure 5E and F) HIV-1LAI induced IL-1β secretion and cell death only in CARD8 KO THP-1 cells that were complemented with WT human CARD8, but not CARD8 mutants that are resistant to HIV-1PR cleavage.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B, C, E, and F.

claim: CARD8 KO THP-1 cells complemented with chimpanzee CARD8 restore responsiveness to VbP but not to HIV-1LAI infection.
source: We also found that CARD8 KO THP-1 cells complemented with chimpanzee CARD8 restored responsiveness to VbP but not to HIV-1LAI infection, whereas chimpanzee CARD8 L60F (i.e. chimpanzee CARD8 with the phenylalanine at residue 60 as in human CARD8) is cleaved by HIV-1PR and SIVcpzPR (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), and can functionally complement human CARD8 responses to HIV-1 infection (Figure 5D–F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D-F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Chimpanzee CARD8 L60F is cleaved by HIV-1PR and SIVcpzPR.
source: We also found that CARD8 KO THP-1 cells complemented with chimpanzee CARD8 restored responsiveness to VbP but not to HIV-1LAI infection, whereas chimpanzee CARD8 L60F (i.e. chimpanzee CARD8 with the phenylalanine at residue 60 as in human CARD8) is cleaved by HIV-1PR and SIVcpzPR (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), and can functionally complement human CARD8 responses to HIV-1 infection (Figure 5D–F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Chimpanzee CARD8 L60F can functionally complement human CARD8 responses to HIV-1 infection.
source: We also found that CARD8 KO THP-1 cells complemented with chimpanzee CARD8 restored responsiveness to VbP but not to HIV-1LAI infection, whereas chimpanzee CARD8 L60F (i.e. chimpanzee CARD8 with the phenylalanine at residue 60 as in human CARD8) is cleaved by HIV-1PR and SIVcpzPR (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), and can functionally complement human CARD8 responses to HIV-1 infection (Figure 5D–F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D-F.

claim: Human CARD8 detects the enzymatic activity of HIVPR by encoding a motif that functions as a HIVPR substrate.
source: Thus, human CARD8 detects the enzymatic activity of HIVPR by encoding a motif that functions as a HIVPR substrate, permitting a human-specific CARD8 inflammasome response to HIV-1 infection.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing the F59-F60 motif is required for HIV-1PR cleavage and inflammasome activation.

claim: The ability to selectively induce CARD8-dependent pyroptosis in HIV-1 latently infected CD4+ T cells via NNRTI-enforced dimerization of HIV-1PR has garnered interest as a means to clear the latent reservoir.
source: The ability to selectively induce CARD8-dependent pyroptosis in HIV-1 latently infected CD4+ T cells via NNRTI-enforced dimerization of HIV-1PR has garnered much interest as a means to clear the latent reservoir (Balibar et al., 2023; Clark et al., 2022; Moore et al., 2022; Sparrer and Kirchhoff, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Balibar et al., 2023; Clark et al., 2022; Moore et al., 2022; Sparrer and Kirchhoff, 2021.

claim: CARD8 senses HIV-1 replication in acutely infected cells.
source: Here, we demonstrate that CARD8 also senses HIV-1 replication in acutely infected cells, which occurs following HIV-1PR site-specific cleavage of a human-specific motif in the CARD8 tripwire.
evidence: Supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript showing CARD8 activation during acute HIV-1 infection.

claim: The unique motif in human CARD8 is not present in other sampled hominoids and Old World monkeys.
source: We further show that the unique motif in human CARD8, which is not present in other sampled hominoids and Old World monkeys, enables its sensing of SIVcpzPR – the precursor to HIV-1, indicating that the precursor viruses to HIV-1 were poised to cleave human CARD8 prior to spillover into humans.
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis and experimental data showing SIVcpzPR cleaves human CARD8.

claim: The precursor viruses to HIV-1 were poised to cleave human CARD8 prior to spillover into humans.
source: We further show that the unique motif in human CARD8, which is not present in other sampled hominoids and Old World monkeys, enables its sensing of SIVcpzPR – the precursor to HIV-1, indicating that the precursor viruses to HIV-1 were poised to cleave human CARD8 prior to spillover into humans.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing SIVcpzPR cleaves human CARD8 but not chimpanzee CARD8.

claim: CARD8 is a bona fide innate immune sensor of viral infection via sensing viral protease activity.
source: These results, along with other recent findings (Nadkarni et al., 2022; Tsu et al., 2023), demonstrate that CARD8 is a bone fide innate immune sensor of viral infection via sensing viral protease activity, and suggest a model for a human-specific inflammatory response to HIV infection.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in this manuscript and citations to Nadkarni et al., 2022; Tsu et al., 2023.

claim: HIV-1 triggers CARD8 inflammasome activation as early as 2 hr post-infection, well before de novo synthesis of viral proteins.
source: However, as HIV-1 triggers CARD8 inflammasome activation as early as 2 hr post-infection, well before de novo synthesis of viral proteins (Figure 4A), our findings suggest that HIV-1 entry is also targeted by CARD8 via the innate immune detection of incoming viral protease activity.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: HIV-1 entry is targeted by CARD8 via the innate immune detection of incoming viral protease activity.
source: However, as HIV-1 triggers CARD8 inflammasome activation as early as 2 hr post-infection, well before de novo synthesis of viral proteins (Figure 4A), our findings suggest that HIV-1 entry is also targeted by CARD8 via the innate immune detection of incoming viral protease activity.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing early CARD8 activation before viral protein synthesis.

claim: HIV-1 strains lacking RT or integrase function are still sensed by the CARD8 inflammasome in a manner dependent on HIV-1PR activity.
source: This conclusion is supported by a recent report that also found that HIV-1 strains lacking RT or integrase function are still sensed by the CARD8 inflammasome in a manner dependent on HIV-1PR activity (Wang and Shan, 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang and Shan, 2023.

claim: CARD8 can sense HIV-1PR that is packaged into the virion upon its release into the host cytosol upon viral fusion.
source: Based on these findings, we propose that CARD8 can sense HIV-1PR that is packaged into the virion upon its release into the host cytosol upon viral fusion.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing early CARD8 activation.

claim: HIV-1PR can function intracellularly to cleave host targets, and not solely in the context of Gag-Pol dimerization during virion assembly and maturation.
source: This idea is consistent with reports that HIV-1PR can function intracellularly to cleave host targets, and not solely in the context of Gag-Pol dimerization during virion assembly and maturation (Alvarez et al., 2006; Tabler et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Alvarez et al., 2006; Tabler et al., 2022.

claim: CARD8's broad antiviral sensing capacity is predicated on its detection of the ubiquitous and essential function of viral proteases.
source: Thus, our present findings, along with other recent examples of innate immune detection of viral protease activity (Nadkarni et al., 2022; Tsu et al., 2023), suggest that CARD8's broad antiviral sensing capacity is predicated on its detection of the ubiquitous and essential function of viral proteases, which are evolutionarily constrained by their requirement to target both viral polyprotein and host targets.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data and citations to Nadkarni et al., 2022; Tsu et al., 2023.

claim: Inflammasome responses downstream of CARD8 are modulated by TLR stimulation.
source: We find that inflammasome responses downstream of CARD8 are modulated by TLR stimulation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing differential responses with and without TLR priming.

claim: CARD8-dependent cell death is modestly enhanced by TLR priming.
source: For example, CARD8-dependent cell death is modestly enhanced by TLR priming by an unknown mechanism (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: IL-1β secretion following HIV-1 infection is strictly dependent on TLR priming.
source: On the other hand, IL-1β secretion following HIV-1 infection is strictly dependent on TLR priming, consistent with its established role for transcriptional upregulation of IL-1β (Chan and Schroder, 2019).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citation to Chan and Schroder, 2019.

claim: HIV-1 pathogen-associated molecular patterns and/or circulating microbial ligands from gut epithelial breakdown are potential sources for priming of HIV-1 target cells in vivo.
source: Our findings that several TLR agonists effectively prime CARD8 inflammasome responses (Figure 3B and C) suggest that HIV-1 pathogen-associated molecular patterns (i.e. viral nucleic acids) and/or circulating microbial ligands from gut epithelial breakdown, a hallmark of acute HIV-1 disease (Sandler and Douek, 2012), are potential sources for priming of HIV-1 target cells in vivo.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data and citation to Sandler and Douek, 2012.

claim: Gut epithelial breakdown is a hallmark of acute HIV-1 disease.
source: Our findings that several TLR agonists effectively prime CARD8 inflammasome responses (Figure 3B and C) suggest that HIV-1 pathogen-associated molecular patterns (i.e. viral nucleic acids) and/or circulating microbial ligands from gut epithelial breakdown, a hallmark of acute HIV-1 disease (Sandler and Douek, 2012), are potential sources for priming of HIV-1 target cells in vivo.
evidence: Supported by citation to Sandler and Douek, 2012.

claim: The F59-F60 motif that confers human CARD8 with the unique capacity to sense HIV/SIVcpzPR is conserved across all humans based on publicly available datasets.
source: The F59-F60 motif that confers human CARD8 with the unique capacity to sense HIV/SIVcpzPR is conserved across all humans based on publicly available datasets, as well as being present in a Neanderthal genome, suggesting a genetic sweep occurred in favor of a phenylalanine at position 60.
evidence: Based on analysis of publicly available genomic datasets.

claim: A genetic sweep occurred in favor of a phenylalanine at position 60 in human CARD8.
source: The F59-F60 motif that confers human CARD8 with the unique capacity to sense HIV/SIVcpzPR is conserved across all humans based on publicly available datasets, as well as being present in a Neanderthal genome, suggesting a genetic sweep occurred in favor of a phenylalanine at position 60.
evidence: Inferred from conservation of the motif across all humans and Neanderthals.

claim: HIV-1 emerged within the past century.
source: HIV-1 emerged within the past century (Sharp and Hahn, 2010) and therefore could not have driven the evolution of the HIV-1PR cleavage site in human CARD8.
evidence: Supported by citation to Sharp and Hahn, 2010.

claim: HIV-1 could not have driven the evolution of the HIV-1PR cleavage site in human CARD8.
source: HIV-1 emerged within the past century (Sharp and Hahn, 2010) and therefore could not have driven the evolution of the HIV-1PR cleavage site in human CARD8.
evidence: Inferred from the timing of HIV-1 emergence relative to the evolution of the F59-F60 motif.

claim: Human CARD8 is highly polymorphic.
source: However, human CARD8 is highly polymorphic, and multiple residues of the N-terminus of CARD8, including those that allow CARD8 sensing of extant human pathogenic viruses including coronaviruses and picornaviruses, show strong evidence of positive selection, an evolutionary signature consistent with a history of host-pathogen conflict (Daugherty and Malik, 2012; Tsu et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to Daugherty and Malik, 2012; Tsu et al., 2023.

claim: Multiple residues of the N-terminus of CARD8 show strong evidence of positive selection.
source: However, human CARD8 is highly polymorphic, and multiple residues of the N-terminus of CARD8, including those that allow CARD8 sensing of extant human pathogenic viruses including coronaviruses and picornaviruses, show strong evidence of positive selection, an evolutionary signature consistent with a history of host-pathogen conflict (Daugherty and Malik, 2012; Tsu et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to Daugherty and Malik, 2012; Tsu et al., 2023.

claim: The HIV-1PR cleavage site in CARD8 overlaps with a site that is cleaved by the coronavirus 3CL protease.
source: Indeed, the HIV-1PR cleavage site in CARD8 overlaps with a site that is cleaved by the coronavirus 3CL protease (Tsu et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tsu et al., 2023.

claim: An ancient infection of human ancestors may be responsible for modern-day maladaptation to HIV-1.
source: Thus, we speculate that an ancient infection of our human ancestors may be responsible for our modern-day maladaptation to HIV-1.
evidence: Speculative inference based on evolutionary analysis and experimental data.

claim: HIV-1 disease progression to AIDS is characterized by dramatic depletion of CD4+ T cells including via pyroptosis.
source: HIV-1 disease progression to AIDS is characterized by dramatic depletion of CD4+ T cells including via pyroptosis (Doitsh et al., 2014) and chronic inflammation accompanied by high levels of plasma cytokines including IL-1 (Arditi et al., 1991; Muema et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Doitsh et al., 2014; Arditi et al., 1991; Muema et al., 2020.

claim: HIV-1 disease progression to AIDS is characterized by chronic inflammation accompanied by high levels of plasma cytokines including IL-1.
source: HIV-1 disease progression to AIDS is characterized by dramatic depletion of CD4+ T cells including via pyroptosis (Doitsh et al., 2014) and chronic inflammation accompanied by high levels of plasma cytokines including IL-1 (Arditi et al., 1991; Muema et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Arditi et al., 1991; Muema et al., 2020.

claim: HIV infection induces pyroptotic cell death and IL-1β secretion via CARD8 recognition of HIVPR activity.
source: Here, we show that HIV infection induces pyroptotic cell death and IL-1β secretion via CARD8 recognition of HIVPR activity.
evidence: Supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: HIV-1 infection is sufficient to induce inflammasome activation.
source: Our finding that HIV-1 infection is sufficient to induce inflammasome activation, along with the presence of CARD8 in relevant T cell populations (Clark et al., 2022; Johnson et al., 2020; Linder et al., 2020), also suggests that CARD8 contributes to HIV pathogenesis.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citations to Clark et al., 2022; Johnson et al., 2020; Linder et al., 2020.

claim: CARD8 is present in relevant T cell populations.
source: Our finding that HIV-1 infection is sufficient to induce inflammasome activation, along with the presence of CARD8 in relevant T cell populations (Clark et al., 2022; Johnson et al., 2020; Linder et al., 2020), also suggests that CARD8 contributes to HIV pathogenesis.
evidence: Supported by citations to Clark et al., 2022; Johnson et al., 2020; Linder et al., 2020.

claim: CARD8 contributes to HIV pathogenesis.
source: Our finding that HIV-1 infection is sufficient to induce inflammasome activation, along with the presence of CARD8 in relevant T cell populations (Clark et al., 2022; Johnson et al., 2020; Linder et al., 2020), also suggests that CARD8 contributes to HIV pathogenesis.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing CARD8-dependent responses to HIV-1 infection.

claim: HIV-1 infection drives CARD8-dependent pyroptotic cell death both in primary human CD4+ T cells ex vivo and in humanized mouse models of HIV-1.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, recent publications show that HIV-1 infection drives CARD8-dependent pyroptotic cell death both in primary human CD4+ T cells ex vivo and in humanized mouse models of HIV-1 (Wang and Shan, 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang and Shan, 2023.

claim: IL-1β induces the differentiation of Th17 cells.
source: It is also possible that IL-1β release after HIV-1-dependent CARD8 activation after HIV-1 infection could contribute to pathogenesis since IL-1β induces the differentiation of Th17 cells (Chung et al., 2009), a highly HIV-susceptible CD4+ T cell subtype, as well as the recruitment of other target immune cells (Rider et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chung et al., 2009.

claim: Th17 cells are a highly HIV-susceptible CD4+ T cell subtype.
source: It is also possible that IL-1β release after HIV-1-dependent CARD8 activation after HIV-1 infection could contribute to pathogenesis since IL-1β induces the differentiation of Th17 cells (Chung et al., 2009), a highly HIV-susceptible CD4+ T cell subtype, as well as the recruitment of other target immune cells (Rider et al., 2011).
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge.

claim: IL-1β induces the recruitment of target immune cells.
source: It is also possible that IL-1β release after HIV-1-dependent CARD8 activation after HIV-1 infection could contribute to pathogenesis since IL-1β induces the differentiation of Th17 cells (Chung et al., 2009), a highly HIV-susceptible CD4+ T cell subtype, as well as the recruitment of other target immune cells (Rider et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rider et al., 2011.

claim: SIVs are believed to be generally non-pathogenic in their reservoir hosts.
source: SIVs are believed to be generally non-pathogenic in their reservoir hosts with the SIVsmm in sooty mangabeys and SIVagm in African green monkeys as the best studied examples (Jasinska et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jasinska et al., 2023.

claim: SIVcpz in naturally infected chimpanzees is pathogenic although not to the extent of HIV-1 group M infection of untreated humans.
source: SIVcpz in naturally infected chimpanzees is pathogenic although not to the extent of HIV-1 group M infection of untreated humans (Keele et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Keele et al., 2009.

claim: SIVs can cause disease in a new species, including experimental SIV infections of macaque monkeys.
source: In contrast, SIVs can cause disease in a new species, including experimental SIV infections of macaque monkeys.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge.

claim: Species-specific differences in SIV pathogenesis could be, in part, mediated by differential CARD8 inflammasome activation.
source: It is tempting to speculate that these species-specific differences could be, in part, mediated by differential CARD8 inflammasome activation, which in turn influences the extent of CD4+ T cell depletion, chronic immune activation, and bystander cell immunopathology – key pathogenic events that drive the progression to AIDS in the absence of antiretroviral therapy (Kaur et al., 1998; Keele et al., 2009; Paiardini and Müller-Trutwin, 2013).
evidence: Speculative inference based on experimental data and citations.

claim: CD4+ T cell depletion, chronic immune activation, and bystander cell immunopathology are key pathogenic events that drive the progression to AIDS in the absence of antiretroviral therapy.
source: It is tempting to speculate that these species-specific differences could be, in part, mediated by differential CARD8 inflammasome activation, which in turn influences the extent of CD4+ T cell depletion, chronic immune activation, and bystander cell immunopathology – key pathogenic events that drive the progression to AIDS in the absence of antiretroviral therapy (Kaur et al., 1998; Keele et al., 2009; Paiardini and Müller-Trutwin, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kaur et al., 1998; Keele et al., 2009; Paiardini and Müller-Trutwin, 2013.

claim: The substrate specificity of SIVmac239PR is distinct from HIV-1PR.
source: Indeed, the substrate specificity of SIVmac239PR is distinct from HIV-1PR (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), which may be relevant to CARD8 inflammasome activation and CD4+ T cell depletion in experimental macaque infections.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: CARD8 consists of a disordered N-terminus, a function-to-find domain (FIIND), and a caspase activation and recruitment domain (CARD).
source: The inflammasome-forming sensor caspase recruitment domain-containing protein 8 (CARD8) consists of a disordered N-terminus, a function-to-find domain (FIIND), and a caspase activation and recruitment domain (CARD) (Taabazuing et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Taabazuing et al., 2020.

claim: The FIIND is comprised of ZU5 and UPA subdomains.
source: The FIIND, comprised of ZU5 and UPA subdomains, undergoes self-cleavage resulting in two non-covalently associated fragments (D'Osualdo et al., 2011; Taabazuing et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to D'Osualdo et al., 2011; Taabazuing et al., 2020.

claim: The FIIND undergoes self-cleavage resulting in two non-covalently associated fragments.
source: The FIIND, comprised of ZU5 and UPA subdomains, undergoes self-cleavage resulting in two non-covalently associated fragments (D'Osualdo et al., 2011; Taabazuing et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to D'Osualdo et al., 2011; Taabazuing et al., 2020.

claim: Proteasome-dependent degradation of the N-terminus leads to the release and assembly of the C-terminal UPA-CARD.
source: Proteasome-dependent degradation of the N-terminus leads to the release and assembly of the C-terminal UPA-CARD, serving as a platform for the recruitment and activation of caspase-1 (CASP1).
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about CARD8 function.

claim: The C-terminal UPA-CARD serves as a platform for the recruitment and activation of caspase-1 (CASP1).
source: Proteasome-dependent degradation of the N-terminus leads to the release and assembly of the C-terminal UPA-CARD, serving as a platform for the recruitment and activation of caspase-1 (CASP1).
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about CARD8 function.

claim: Activated CASP1 initiates pyroptosis and the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines including IL-1β and IL-18.
source: Activated CASP1 initiates a lytic, programmed cell death called pyroptosis and the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines including interleukin (IL)-1β and IL-18 (Broz and Dixit, 2016; Fink and Cookson, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Broz and Dixit, 2016; Fink and Cookson, 2005.

claim: DPP8/9 form an inhibitory complex with CARD8 to prevent aberrant release of the UPA-CARD.
source: To prevent aberrant release of the UPA-CARD, the dipeptidyl peptidases 8 and 9 (DPP8/9) form an inhibitory complex with CARD8 (Sharif et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sharif et al., 2021.

claim: Direct inhibition of DPP8/9 by Val-boroPro causes CARD8 inflammasome activation.
source: For example, disruptions to protein homeostasis, including direct (e.g. Val-boroPro) and indirect (e.g. CQ31) inhibition of DPP8/9, cause CARD8 inflammasome activation (Johnson et al., 2020; Johnson et al., 2018; Rao et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Johnson et al., 2020; Johnson et al., 2018; Rao et al., 2022.

claim: Indirect inhibition of DPP8/9 by CQ31 causes CARD8 inflammasome activation.
source: For example, disruptions to protein homeostasis, including direct (e.g. Val-boroPro) and indirect (e.g. CQ31) inhibition of DPP8/9, cause CARD8 inflammasome activation (Johnson et al., 2020; Johnson et al., 2018; Rao et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Johnson et al., 2020; Johnson et al., 2018; Rao et al., 2022.

claim: Treatment of HIV-1 latently infected cells with certain NNRTIs enforces the cytosolic dimerization of the HIV-1PR and results in CARD8 inflammasome activation.
source: For example, treatment of HIV-1 latently infected cells with certain nonnucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs), including efavirenz (Wang et al., 2021) or doravirine-like analogs including the pyrimidines Pyr01 (Balibar et al., 2023), enforce the cytosolic dimerization of the HIV-1PR and results in CARD8 inflammasome activation in primary CD4+ T cells and humanized mouse models (Clark et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wang et al., 2021; Balibar et al., 2023; Clark et al., 2022.

claim: HIV-1PR cleavage of the N-terminus of CARD8 causes proteasome-dependent degradation of the CARD8 N-terminal fragment.
source: HIV-1PR cleavage of the N-terminus of CARD8 causes proteasome-dependent degradation of the CARD8 N-terminal fragment (Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2021.

claim: Functional degradation of CARD8 N-terminus liberates the UPA-CARD fragment for inflammasome assembly and activation.
source: This 'functional degradation' liberates the UPA-CARD fragment for inflammasome assembly and activation, analogous to viral protease sensing by the inflammasome-forming sensor NLRP1 (Robinson et al., 2020; Sandstrom et al., 2019; Tsu et al., 2021a; Tsu et al., 2021b; Planès et al., 2022) in which the N-terminus of CARD8 functions as a molecular 'tripwire' to sense and respond to the enzymatic activity of HIV-1PR and other viral proteases (Castro and Daugherty, 2023; Nadkarni et al., 2022; Tsu et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to Robinson et al., 2020; Sandstrom et al., 2019; Tsu et al., 2021a; Tsu et al., 2021b; Planès et al., 2022; Castro and Daugherty, 2023; Nadkarni et al., 2022; Tsu et al., 2023.

claim: The N-terminus of CARD8 functions as a molecular 'tripwire' to sense and respond to the enzymatic activity of HIV-1PR and other viral proteases.
source: This 'functional degradation' liberates the UPA-CARD fragment for inflammasome assembly and activation, analogous to viral protease sensing by the inflammasome-forming sensor NLRP1 (Robinson et al., 2020; Sandstrom et al., 2019; Tsu et al., 2021a; Tsu et al., 2021b; Planès et al., 2022) in which the N-terminus of CARD8 functions as a molecular 'tripwire' to sense and respond to the enzymatic activity of HIV-1PR and other viral proteases (Castro and Daugherty, 2023; Nadkarni et al., 2022; Tsu et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to Castro and Daugherty, 2023; Nadkarni et al., 2022; Tsu et al., 2023.

claim: Priming of target cells via TLR agonists prior to HIV-1 challenge enhances CARD8-dependent cell death.
source: We find that priming of target cells via Toll-like receptor (TLR) agonists prior to HIV-1 challenge enhances CARD8-dependent cell death and is required for IL-1β secretion.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Priming of target cells via TLR agonists prior to HIV-1 challenge is required for IL-1β secretion.
source: We find that priming of target cells via Toll-like receptor (TLR) agonists prior to HIV-1 challenge enhances CARD8-dependent cell death and is required for IL-1β secretion.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: CARD8 sensing of HIV-1 and other simian lentiviruses is dependent on a F59-F60 motif in human CARD8.
source: Our evolution-guided studies reveal that CARD8 sensing of HIV-1 and other simian lentiviruses is dependent on a F59-F60 motif in human CARD8 that permits its sensing of HIV-1PR.
evidence: Supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The F59-F60 motif is absent in other primates that serve as reservoirs of simian immunodeficiency viruses (SIVs).
source: This motif is absent in other primates that serve as reservoirs of simian immunodeficiency viruses (SIVs), and although both HIV-1PR and SIVcpzPR cleave and activate human CARD8, we find that neither are sensed by chimpanzee CARD8.
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis and experimental data.

claim: Both HIV-1PR and SIVcpzPR cleave and activate human CARD8.
source: This motif is absent in other primates that serve as reservoirs of simian immunodeficiency viruses (SIVs), and although both HIV-1PR and SIVcpzPR cleave and activate human CARD8, we find that neither are sensed by chimpanzee CARD8.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Neither HIV-1PR nor SIVcpzPR are sensed by chimpanzee CARD8.
source: This motif is absent in other primates that serve as reservoirs of simian immunodeficiency viruses (SIVs), and although both HIV-1PR and SIVcpzPR cleave and activate human CARD8, we find that neither are sensed by chimpanzee CARD8.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The CARD8 inflammasome functions in the innate immune detection of HIV-1 replication.
source: Thus, our study reveals that the CARD8 inflammasome functions in the innate immune detection of HIV-1 replication.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing CARD8-dependent responses to HIV-1 infection.

claim: The evolution of the F59-F60 motif in humans gave rise to a human-specific host-virus interaction following the spillover of SIVcpz into humans.
source: Moreover, our findings suggest that the evolution of the F59-F60 motif in humans gave rise to a human-specific host-virus interaction following the spillover of SIVcpz into humans, which may uniquely shape human innate immune responses to lentiviral infection.
evidence: Inferred from evolutionary analysis and experimental data.

claim: The evolution of the F59-F60 motif may uniquely shape human innate immune responses to lentiviral infection.
source: Moreover, our findings suggest that the evolution of the F59-F60 motif in humans gave rise to a human-specific host-virus interaction following the spillover of SIVcpz into humans, which may uniquely shape human innate immune responses to lentiviral infection.
evidence: Speculative inference based on experimental data and evolutionary analysis.
